parts:
Hello Haris
Those are fairly big questions. Starting with the easy one: yes, you need cartesian coordinates, and I'm sure QGIS can do that for you - just project to any cartesian system e.g. UTM. Even if you're not used to R, this may help.

I am guessing that you collected hair samples and identified individuals by DNA? It is important to allow for big differences in search effort, but this is simple enough in the software.

A SECR model fitted to data from a narrow region can certainly be extrapolated to a wider region; whether that 'makes sense' is a matter of biological judgement.
fying.

DENSITY is limited (and certainly doesn't fit open population models). You really should overcome your fear of R! The online interface to the R package gets you halfway there, but probably it won't be very satisfying as you really have to grasp how 'secr' works to make the most of it.

Murray
On Sunday, December 11, 2022 at 10:43:39 PM UTC+13 pil...@hotmail.co.uk wrote:

Hello everyone,

I hope my message finds you well. Thank you admins for approving my request to join the group!

The SECR method has been under my radar for a while. I am working on the population estimation of the East Balkan distribution of brown bears (Bulgaria and Greece) and I am excited about the potential of using the DENSITY software.

—Our team has sampled a subset of the permanent East Balkan distribution of brown bears (dark green areas in circled area below) over 3 years in a row.


— Some areas were sampled intensively in short sampling sessions. In the right map shared above the white green dots are collected samples and the white are captures and recaptures (no sex information available)

I was hoping to ask the group for some guidance on how to proceed and specifically how could we determine which model we can use. I like the idea of using both closed and open models and comparing (I can feel some eyebrows raising already!)

—I like the idea of only using grids where sampling was intensive and extapolating for the whole distribution

—I also like the idea of weighing the results within each sampling grid/trap/sampling year based on the number/density of collected samples. Is there a way to do this?

—Also do I need to convert my coordinates from geographic to Cartesian and is there a way to do it on QGIS? A lot of the example files use geographic coordinates (but then the software cannot read those files unless I am doing something wrong…)

It would be great to have your thoughts on the above. I should add that I am using the DENSITY v5 software as I don’t use R (and there is no sufficient time to learn within our time frame for producing the results). Finally -and I hope it is OK to add this- we are very much open to discussing collaborating towards a potential publication with anyone more familiar with the method and package and interested in helping with getting the analysis running.

Thank you very much,

Haris
